The rain begins again without ceremony, as if the sky had simply remembered it was unfinished. It taps on the windowpane in uneven rhythms, then settles into a steady hush, and somewhere outside a streetlamp flickers to life, casting its small gold circle on the wet pavement.

I have always liked the idea that silence is not empty. It is full of things waiting to be heard: the creak of a floorboard, the distant sound of a train, the faint hum of a refrigerator in another room. The world does not stop being alive just because no one is speaking.

Perhaps that is why I keep returning to small moments. A cup of tea cooling in my hands. A book left open on a chair. The way light changes in the afternoon and makes ordinary objects look important, as though they have been waiting all day to be seen.

There are days when I want to say something grand. I want to write about oceans, mountains, the distance between stars, the strange luck of being alive. But more often the truth is smaller than that. It lives in the pause between one breath and the next, in the decision to go on, in the quiet confidence that tomorrow will ask nothing of us except to begin again.

So I write freely now, not because I have something profound to say, but because I want to leave a mark in the air: a line, a sentence, a small window opening onto a place I might have forgotten how to name.

Here, then, is the thing I am writing about: the world arriving as it always does, unexpected, unrepeatable, and full of ordinary grace.
